title: What can a pot tell us about an early community?
essentialQuestion: What can objects tell us about people who left no writing, and what can they not tell us?
learningGoal: Tell an observation from an inference about a pot from Ban Chiang, and explain why the place where a find lay matters.

warmUp.question: If you found an old pot in the ground, what would you want to know first?
options: What was found next to it

evidence.question: Which details are about the pot itself, and which are about where things were found?

cards.title: Three real sources about Ban Chiang

sources.caption: Source 1: UNESCO's description of the Ban Chiang Archaeological Site (a modern heritage record)
details: Written by UNESCO, a part of the United Nations, for the World Heritage List.
It says Ban Chiang, in northeast Thailand, is a mound built up by people who lived there over a long time.
It says people lived there and also buried their dead there. The layers hold a lot of pottery, and graves held pottery and metal objects.
It says there is early evidence of rice farming and of making bronze.
It says the site's dates have been changed over time, as ways of dating improved.
Limit: it is a modern summary. It was not written by people who lived at Ban Chiang.

sources.caption: Source 2: An article in the Penn Museum's magazine, Expedition, from 1995
details: The Penn Museum (in the United States) and Thailand's Fine Arts Department dug at Ban Chiang in 1974 and 1975.
It says the most important thing to record is context: where each find lay in the ground, and what was near it.
It says artists drew plans (looking down on the site) and sections (the layers seen from the side).
It says the layers were often not clear, and one layer could hold signs of both house life and burials.
Limit: it was written in 1995. Some of its dates are older views that researchers have since changed.

sources.caption: Source 3: A photo of a pot in a museum at Ban Chiang, taken in 2013 by Kiwiodysee
details: It shows one tall clay pot with painted swirls, standing on a stand in a museum display.
Limit: it does not show where the pot was found, which layer it came from, or who made it.

cards.title: Some dates in the Ban Chiang story

events.text: People live, farm and bury their dead at Ban Chiang. Experts still discuss the exact dates.
Pots are seen in a village path, and the site becomes known to researchers.
Thailand's Fine Arts Department and the Penn Museum excavate the site.
UNESCO adds Ban Chiang to the World Heritage List.
Kiwiodysee photographs a pot in a museum at Ban Chiang.

sections.heading: A clue from the ground
sections.text: Ban Chiang is a village in northeast Thailand. Under it is a low hill, or mound, built up by people who lived there long ago. Archaeologists have found pottery, graves and metal objects there. UNESCO says the people of Ban Chiang farmed rice and knew how to make bronze, a metal, very early. These people left no writing, so objects are our main clues. A pot is an artefact: an object that people made or used. We can observe its shape and its painted marks. We cannot see what its maker thought, or every way people used it.
sections.simpler: Ban Chiang is a village in Thailand. Under it is a low hill of earth. People lived there long ago. Archaeologists found pots, graves and metal things there. The people grew rice. They made bronze, a kind of metal. They left no writing. So objects are our clues. A pot is an artefact. People made it and used it. We can see its shape. We cannot see what the maker thought.

sections.heading: Why the findspot matters
sections.text: In 1974 and 1975, the Penn Museum in the United States and Thailand's Fine Arts Department dug at Ban Chiang. This careful digging and recording is called an excavation. The team recorded each find's context: where it lay in the ground and what was near it. Artists drew plans, which look down on the site, and sections, which show the layers from the side. Ban Chiang was a village and also a burial place. The layers were not always neat, and one layer could hold signs of both. So a pot found in a grave raises different questions from a pot found near a house.
sections.simpler: In 1974 and 1975, teams from Thailand and the United States dug at Ban Chiang. This careful digging is called an excavation. The teams wrote down the context of each find. That means where it was in the ground, and what was near it. People lived at Ban Chiang. People were buried there too. The layers were not always neat. A pot from a grave makes us ask different questions.

sections.heading: Look at the real pot
sections.text: The second picture is a photo of one pot in a museum at Ban Chiang, taken in 2013. Start with observations: things you can see, such as its shape and its painted swirls. Then make an inference: an idea that might explain what you see. For example, someone chose to decorate this pot, because the pattern is there. But the photo cannot tell us who made the pot or which layer it came from. A museum label or an excavation record could help. When new evidence appears, historians change their ideas. Even the dates for Ban Chiang have changed over time.
sections.simpler: The second picture is a photo of one pot in a museum. The photo is from 2013. First, say what you see. The pot has painted lines. Then make an inference. That is an idea that explains what you see. Someone chose to paint this pot. But the photo does not show who made it. It does not show where it was found. New evidence can change our ideas. Even the dates for Ban Chiang have changed.

glossary.definition: An object that people made or used, often long ago.
glossary.example: A painted pot from Ban Chiang is an artefact.

glossary.definition: Careful digging at a site, while writing down everything that is found.
glossary.example: The excavation at Ban Chiang took place in 1974 and 1975.

glossary.definition: Where something was found, and what was found near it.
glossary.example: The context of a pot tells us if it lay in a grave or near a house.

glossary.definition: An idea that explains what you see, which more evidence can test.
glossary.example: "Someone chose to decorate this pot" is an inference from its painted marks.

checks.question: Look at the pot in the photo. Which sentence is an observation?

options.text: The owner of the pot was a farmer.
options.feedback: Not quite. Nothing in the photo shows who owned the pot. We would need more evidence. Look at the third part of the reading.

options.text: The pot has painted swirls on it.
options.feedback: Yes. You can see the painted marks in the photo. An observation is something you can see or measure.

options.text: The pot was made for a special day.
options.feedback: Not quite. That is an idea to test, not something you can see. Look again at what the photo shows.

checks.question: Why do archaeologists record where a find lay in the ground?

options.text: To find out the name of the person who made it
options.feedback: Not quite. Context helps, but it still might not tell us who made it. Look at the second part of the reading.

options.text: To make a museum display look better
options.feedback: Not quite. The record is for studying the site, not for a display. Look at the second part of the reading.

options.text: To link it to its layer and nearby finds
options.feedback: Yes. Its context helps us ask how it was used and when. It still does not make every guess certain.

checks.question: What else would you want to know about where this pot was found?
checks.placeholder: I would want to know if ... because ...

write.prompt: Look at the pot in the photo. Write one thing you see, one inference with the word "might", and one question that needs another source.
sentenceStarters: I can see that the pot ...
To know more, I would ask ...
selfCheck: I wrote one thing I can see in the photo.
I wrote one inference with the word "might".
I asked one question that needs another source.
write.example: I can see that the pot has a wide mouth and a round body. Another thing I notice is that it has painted swirls and lines all over it. I can also see cracks, so it might have been broken and put back together. The pot might have had a special use. I think this because someone took time to paint it with care. To know more, I would ask: what else was found next to this pot in the ground?

speak.partnerTask: With a partner, give two different ideas about how the pot was used. Say what evidence would help you choose between them.
speak.independentTask: Say or write three short sentences: one idea about how the pot was used, a second idea, and the evidence that would help you decide.

watch.title: Ban Chiang Archaeological Site (UNESCO/NHK)
watch.why: It is UNESCO's own short film about the Ban Chiang site, so learners can see the place the lesson's evidence comes from.
watch.beforeQuestion: What kinds of objects do you expect to see in a film about a very old village site?
watch.afterQuestion: Pick one object the film shows. Write one thing you can observe about it and one inference about it.
watch.summary: This is a short film by UNESCO and NHK, a Japanese broadcaster. It is about the Ban Chiang site in northeast Thailand. UNESCO's description of the film makes some big claims. It says the site has the earliest evidence in the region of farming. It says the site also has the earliest evidence of making and using metal. Think about these claims as you watch. Words like "earliest" are claims, not observations. They depend on the evidence found so far. Researchers have changed the dates for Ban Chiang over time. So a careful viewer asks two questions. What evidence supports each claim? Could new evidence change it?
keyPoints: UNESCO's description says Ban Chiang has very early evidence of farming and of making metal.
Words like "earliest" are claims that depend on the evidence found so far.
Researchers have changed the dates for Ban Chiang over time.
watch.contentNote: Not yet watched by a person. Title and channel confirmed with YouTube's oEmbed on 1 November 2026. YouTube's own page and captions could not be read from here, so the length is unknown and the summary is based only on UNESCO's record for the film (whc.unesco.org/en/documents/103960: English, 20 June 2011, © NHK, re-use needs NHK's permission), not on its words. That record calls Ban Chiang the most important prehistoric settlement so far discovered in South-East Asia, with the earliest evidence of farming and metal in the region: a sweeping "earliest" claim, while UNESCO's listing now says the site's dating has been adjusted over time. Frame it as a claim. Preview it for any images of graves or human remains, and for adverts.

reflect.completionMessage: You finished Lesson 1. You told an observation from an inference, and explained why a find's context matters.

visual.description: "How context helps": a schematic cross-section of the ground, with the words "schematic, not a real trench" in one corner. Three soil layers drawn as wavy bands that blend into each other at their edges (not neat slices), with the top edge labelled "ground today". In the middle layer, one simple pot (a plain outline, not a copy of a real Ban Chiang pattern) with a few broken pieces near it. Three tags with short lines pointing to parts of the drawing: "found: a pot in layer 2" (with a tick), "measured: depth and position" (with a small ruler beside a dashed depth line), and "inferred: an idea to test" (with a question mark, pointing to a dotted thought bubble that reads "used for storing food?"). A small key: "found and measured = recorded", "inferred = still a question". No skeletons, no bodies, no people, and no drawing of a particular grave.
visual.alt: A simple drawing of layers of earth with a pot in the middle layer. Labels show what was found (the pot), what was measured (its depth and position) and what is only inferred (an idea about its use, with a question mark).
visual.caption: A simple diagram made for this lesson. It is not a real trench at Ban Chiang. It shows a find, a measurement and an idea to test.
visual.lookClosely: Which labels describe what was found, and which describe an idea to test?

secondVisual.description: Wikimedia Commons file "Ban Chiang Museum Ceramic Pot.JPG", a photo by Kiwiodysee (own work), taken on 7 September 2013. It shows one tall clay pot with a wide, flared mouth, painted with red-brown swirls and curving lines on a pale surface, on a thin metal stand in a museum display, with another pot behind it and a small label at the lower right. Cracks show it has been put back together. Chosen because learners can make clear observations of shape and decoration, while the museum setting hides the find's context, which is the lesson's point. The file page describes it as a pot of the "neolithic Ban Chiang culture"; the lesson does not repeat that label.
secondVisual.alt: A tall clay pot with a wide, flared mouth, covered in red-brown painted swirls and curving lines on a pale background. It stands on a thin metal stand in a museum display, and cracks run across its body.
secondVisual.caption: A clay pot on display in a museum at Ban Chiang, photographed in 2013. The photo shows one object, not every pot from the site, and not where this pot was found.
secondVisual.lookClosely: Name two features you can see. What would you need to know about where it was found?

sensitiveNotes: Ban Chiang was a burial place as well as a village. The lesson names graves plainly and shows no human remains; keep discussion on objects and context, and preview the film for burials. Never ask learners about their own or their family's experiences, home country, religion or ethnicity; ideas about how the pot was used stay about Ban Chiang.
educatorNotes: Aim: learners separate an observation from a careful inference about one artefact, and say what its context could add. Evidence move: ask what the museum photo leaves out about the pot's excavation context (its layer, what lay near it, grave or house area). A sound answer gives an observation, a tentative inference with "might", and a specific source to look for. Invite "we don't know yet" as a good answer.

Misconception to address: a museum display photo is not a photo of the object where it was found, and neither "all pots were for burial" nor "this pot belonged to a farmer" follows from it. Source caveats: avoid any "first ever" date; UNESCO says the site's dating has been adjusted as radiometric dating improved, and the 1995 Penn article (which the Penn Museum flags as a historical reference) gives older date ranges, so the lesson says only "more than 2,000 years ago". The photo is an example; nothing says which trench this pot came from.
changes: Written on 1 November 2026 from Justin's course brief (28 October 2026), sections 3 and 3A.
Used the British spelling "artefact" (as in Our World's Lesson 2) for the brief's "artifact".

Added from UNESCO's listing (opened 1 November 2026) that the people of Ban Chiang farmed rice and made bronze very early, and that its dating has been adjusted, so the Watch summary's facts are all in Read. Gave no start date: UNESCO and the 1995 Penn article give different ranges, so the timeline says only "more than 2,000 years ago".

The 1966 discovery, the 1974–1975 excavations and the 1992 World Heritage listing come from the 1995 Penn article; UNESCO's page also says the site was first found in 1966. The Penn Museum's project page now says little beyond the 1974–1975 excavations with the Fine Arts Department.

Commons file checked through the Commons API on 1 November 2026: Kiwiodysee, own work, taken 7 September 2013, CC BY-SA 3.0, as the brief says. The museum is not named on the file page, so institution is null. Alt text written from the image itself (it also shows cracks where the pot was repaired).
